question: What is the main goal of psychological therapy when caring for someone with a progressive, degenerative illness?

options.A: To reverse the physical damage to brain tissues
options.B: To replace the need for physical and occupational therapy
options.C: To cure the underlying disease process completely
options.D: To help patients and families cope with ongoing changes

explanation: Since these conditions can't be reversed, therapy is all about emotional support and helping everyone adjust. You've got this! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T18#GNS222_U4_T18_h1)

question: Why is it so helpful to introduce psychological support early after a degenerative diagnosis?

options.A: It helps patients adapt before severe cognitive decline sets in
options.B: It eliminates the need for any future medical interventions
options.C: It stops the physical degeneration from spreading to organs
options.D: It guarantees complete recovery from emotional distress

explanation: Starting early means patients can still clearly express their thoughts and take part in planning their own care. Great nursing insight to keep in mind! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T18#GNS222_U4_T18_h1)

question: What do we mean when we say a family caregiver is experiencing 'anticipatory grief'?

options.A: Grief experienced in anticipation of future losses and decline
options.B: Denial that the family member is actually sick
options.C: Grief felt after the patient has already passed away
options.D: Anger directed at medical staff for failing to find a cure

explanation: Anticipatory grief is that heavy heart a family feels as they watch a loved one slowly lose abilities over time. It's completely natural. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T18#GNS222_U4_T18_h2)

question: A family caregiver feels super guilty just for wanting a single day off. What does this most likely point to?

options.A: The caregiver has completely abandoned the patient
options.B: The patient needs immediate admission to an intensive care unit
options.C: The caregiver is experiencing normal caregiver burnout and emotional strain
options.D: The caregiver is showing signs of physical infection

explanation: Caring for someone takes a massive emotional toll. Feeling guilty for needing a breather is a classic sign of burnout—remember to care for the caregivers too! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T18#GNS222_U4_T18_h2)

question: What is the main purpose of doing a baseline psychiatric assessment for a patient with a degenerative illness?

options.A: To diagnose the exact genetic mutation causing the disease
options.B: To establish a baseline for the patient's mood and cognitive status
options.C: To replace the need for a physical neurological examination
options.D: To test the patient's physical strength and balance

explanation: Taking a baseline measurement lets us see where the patient stands today, so we can track any mental or emotional changes later on. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T18#GNS222_U4_T18_h3)

question: Why must nurses tailor assessment tools to fit a degenerative patient's physical limits?

options.A: To make the test results legally binding in a court of law
options.B: To eliminate the need for family members to be present
options.C: To ensure the patient does not get tired or frustrated during testing
options.D: To reduce the financial cost of purchasing paper questionnaires

explanation: If a patient is exhausted, test scores won't show their true ability. Matching their energy levels keeps the assessment accurate and stress-free. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T18#GNS222_U4_T18_h3)

question: What is the core focus of Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) when managing chronic health conditions?

options.A: Changing unhelpful thought patterns and building practical coping skills
options.B: Using high doses of medication to alter brain chemistry permanently
options.C: Healing past childhood trauma unrelated to the current illness
options.D: Physically strengthening damaged muscle fibers through exercise

explanation: CBT is all about spotting negative thoughts and swapping them for healthy coping habits to make everyday life a little easier. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T18#GNS222_U4_T18_h4)

question: How does breaking big, complicated tasks into tiny steps help a patient with a degenerative condition?

options.A: It speeds up the rate of cognitive processing in the brain
options.B: It ensures the patient never needs assistance from family members
options.C: It prevents feelings of overwhelming helplessness and promotes a sense of control
options.D: It cures the underlying muscle weakness completely

explanation: Mini-steps make daily activities feel doable rather than scary, helping patients hold onto their independence and confidence. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T18#GNS222_U4_T18_h4)

question: What is one of the biggest perks for a patient joining a disease-specific support group?

options.A: It replaces the need for professional medical consultations
options.B: It reduces feelings of isolation by connecting people with similar challenges
options.C: It completely stops the progression of the degenerative disease
options.D: It provides financial compensation for medical bills

explanation: Support groups remind patients and families that they are never walking this difficult road alone. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T18#GNS222_U4_T18_h5)

question: Why is family counseling so valuable when coping with a progressive illness?

options.A: It forces family members to move into the same household
options.B: It eliminates all future disagreements about financial matters
options.C: It helps resolve conflicts and adjust roles regarding care responsibilities
options.D: It proves which family member caused the inherited genetic mutation

explanation: As illnesses progress, family roles shift. Counseling gives everyone a safe space to talk openly and share the care burden smoothly. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T18#GNS222_U4_T18_h5)

question: Near the end of life, what is the primary focus of palliative psychological care?

options.A: Finding a sudden cure for the advanced condition
options.B: Promoting comfort, dignity, and emotional peace
options.C: Preventing family members from visiting the patient

explanation: Palliative care centers entirely on quality of life, surrounding the patient with warmth, respect, and peace. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T18#GNS222_U4_T18_h6)

question: As a student nurse, which action best supports a patient receiving end-of-life palliative care?

options.A: Focusing strictly on lab results rather than emotional needs
options.B: Listening openly to their fears and helping them find personal meaning
options.C: Telling them not to worry about dying and changing the subject
options.D: Restricting family visits to keep the patient completely isolated

explanation: Being a compassionate listener and validating a patient's feelings offers immense comfort during their final days. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T18#GNS222_U4_T18_h6)

question: Which of these is NOT a good nursing intervention for supporting a patient's mental health?

options.A: Monitoring for signs of depression or anxiety
options.B: Creating a chaotic and unpredictable daily ward routine
options.C: Connecting exhausted caregivers with respite resources
options.D: Practicing active listening and therapeutic communication

explanation: Calm and predictable environments soothe anxiety, whereas chaos only adds unnecessary stress for patients with degenerative conditions. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T18#GNS222_U4_T18_h7)

question: You notice a primary family caregiver looks completely exhausted and tearful during visiting hours. What is your best nursing move?

options.A: Admit the caregiver as a patient into the intensive care unit
options.B: Assess the situation and offer information on respite care options
options.C: Ignore the behavior since it is outside the hospital's responsibility
options.D: Scold the caregiver for not handling stress better

explanation: Spotting caregiver burnout and pointing them toward respite care protects the family's health and keeps them strong for their loved one. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T18#GNS222_U4_T18_h7)
